entries.label: resting
entries.reason: Sitting on something people sit on, at a kind that states no stay of its own below: three to ten minutes, long enough to rest and short enough to be seen getting up. A person whose need has reached 750 sits before anything else and is relieved of 500, the figures the society was released with, so how tired people get is unchanged. A rested person sometimes sits too, because in a square people sit to watch, not only when tired: somebody who is not stopping to talk picks among rest, visit and stand by their weights, and rest has 700 of the 2,000 the three share when all three have room.

entries.label: resting on a bench
entries.reason: A bench with a back is the seat people stay on longest in the open: five to fifteen minutes, long enough to rest their legs and watch the square, rarely more than a quarter of an hour. It relieves what any rest relieves; weight and need are the rest entry's.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: resting on a planter seat
entries.reason: A low planter wall with no back is a perch: people sit on it three to ten minutes, a little less long than on a bench. It relieves what any rest relieves; weight and need are the rest entry's.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: sitting at a cafe table
entries.reason: A table with chairs keeps people longest of anything in a square: ten to twenty-five minutes, the time a drink or a snack takes. It relieves what any rest relieves; weight and need are the rest entry's.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: visiting
entries.reason: Stopping at something to look at, at a kind that states no stay of its own below: one to three minutes, a look in passing. It relieves 20 of the need as the released visit did. At 1,000 of the 2,000 weight rest, visit and stand share when all three have room, a rested person who is not stopping to talk most often goes to look at something.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: at a market stall
entries.reason: People at a stall browse its counter and are served: two to six minutes. It relieves what any visit relieves; weight and need are the visit entry's.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: by a tree
entries.reason: People stop by a tree in passing and stand in its shade a minute or a few: one to four minutes. It relieves what any visit relieves; weight and need are the visit entry's.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: standing
entries.reason: Some people just stop and stand: one to four minutes at an open spot within six metres, a few steps from where they are, never on or beside a place somebody uses. Standing rests nobody's legs, so it relieves nothing. At 300 of the 2,000 weight rest, visit and stand share when all three have room, it is the least often chosen of the three.

licence.content_source: Authored for the Exulanica purposeful society; see the entry reason

entries.label: talking
entries.reason: Two people stop and talk: two to six minutes, long enough for a greeting and a few exchanges and short enough that the square keeps changing. The other person is within eight metres, near enough to recognise and call out to, the distance the v3 society lets one inhabitant hear another. They stand at most two metres apart, the close phase of social distance (about 1.2 to 2.1 metres, Hall 1966): on the society's 2 m lattice, two neighbouring nodes joined by an edge, so nothing stands between them. Nothing is said in the simulation and nothing is kept of it; it relieves nothing. Before anybody picks anything else in a minute, each rested person free to choose draws once over all four activities' weights whether to look for somebody to talk to: talk's 500 of 2,500 is one draw in five. One who draws anything else, or finds nobody, then picks among rest, visit and stand by their own weights.
